slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing before cutting hours; with store exits, margin reaches 2.5% by FY2028, 3.0% with targeted hours
Margin fell 2.35 percentage points in two years, mostly in gross margin and e-commerce, not wages
–	Gross margin and e-commerce explain 79% of it; labor 13%
–	Promotions and shrink cost $18M of FY2025 gross profit
Promotions and shrink are the biggest fix: a promotion reset adds $9.9M a year; hour cuts raise shrink
–	Promotions hit 29% of sales, yet 41% call Harlow expensive
–	ValuMart's pressure is local; chain-wide promotions do not pay
E-commerce and nine weak stores lose $13.5M a year; delivery pricing and store exits recover $9.1M
–	Counted in full, e-commerce loses $10.4M a year
–	The tested delivery fee cuts that loss by $2.5M
No-capital moves first protect the covenant; the plan reaches 2.5% by FY2028, 3.0% with targeted hours
–	The 2027 wage rise cuts FY2028 margin from 3.0% to 2.5%
–	Management's hours cut leaves FY2028 margin at 1.0–1.5%

▪	Promotional mix: 29% of sales now sell on promotion, up from 24%, each dollar at 14 percentage points less margin; vendor funding fell from 55% to 46% of markdowns

The reset is cautious: it removes fewer than half of the money-losing events
▪	38% of FY2025 events lost money after counting their extra units; if events are similar in size they carry about 11 percentage points of sales, more than twice the 5 to remove
▪	Dropping an event that loses money raises profit by definition; the risk is traffic, which belongs in ValuMart trade areas
▪	The 14 percentage-point margin gap holds; winning vendor funding back from 46% toward 55% of markdowns is upside, not counted
▪	Each percentage point of promotional share left in place costs about $1.98M a year

slides.title: Counted in full, e-commerce loses $10.4M a year; the team's reported profit leaves out delivery and cannibalization

paragraphs.text: 1 Diagnosis    2 Gross margin    3 Losses    4 Plan
Counted in full, e-commerce loses $10.4M a year; the team's reported profit leaves out delivery and cannibalization
E-commerce cost less contribution from new sales, $ millions, FY2025
Delivery drives the loss, and most online spend is not new
▪	Delivery net of fees: the carrier costs $13.80 per delivered order and the fee brings in $3.10; the team's 6.1% margin leaves it out
▪	Contribution from new sales: 70% of online spend would have been spent in a Harlow store anyway (survey of 2,300 customers)
▪	Per order: a delivered order loses about $12.34 and a click-and-collect order $1.64, so growth in delivery deepens the loss
1  Picking = 1,331,000 orders × $7.40; delivery = 772,000 delivered orders × ($13.80 − $3.10); together they reproduce the $18.1M e-commerce fulfillment line (backup)
2  Contribution = $127.8M e-commerce sales × 30% new to Harlow × 20 cents per new dollar (finance)
Sources: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

slides.title: Rolling out the tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.5M a year and keep the service

paragraphs.text: 1 Diagnosis    2 Gross margin    3 Losses    4 Plan
Rolling out the tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.5M a year and keep the service
Operating-income gain from the delivery-fee rollout, $ millions a year, at FY2025 volumes
lower picking and delivery cost net of fees: delivered orders −9%, click-and-collect +14%, $6.40 fee per delivered order (fee test)
contribution lost on 2% lower e-commerce sales, all treated as new to Harlow
smaller e-commerce loss a year, with delivery still offered
The test is small, so the rollout should be tracked against it
▪	The 4-store, 10-week result holds network-wide: a $7.99 fee and free delivery from $100, instead of $4.99 and $75
▪	Picking stays at $7.40 an order and the carrier at $13.80; its proposed 3% rise is counted separately in the plan
▪	Treating every lost sale as new overstates the cost: at the survey's 30% new share it would be about $0.15M
▪	After the rollout e-commerce still costs about $7.96M a year: carrier terms and a shift to click-and-collect come next
1  The owners want delivery kept in some form; repricing keeps it while 98% of e-commerce sales stay in the test
Sources: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis

slides.title: Exiting the nine loss-making stores would add about $6.6M a year; six leases end by 2027 without a board vote

Exiting the nine loss-making stores would add about $6.6M a year; six leases end by 2027 without a board vote

Three of the nine need a board vote and use $7.5M of the $25M capital limit
▪	Six leases end by the end of 2027 and can be exited as they lapse
▪	The other three need a board vote and a one-time $7.5M lease exit, leaving $17.5M of the limit
▪	Split evenly, those three add about $2.21M a year and pay back the exit cost in about 3.4 years
▪	The exits remove $88.5M of sales, which lowers the sales base for the 3.0% target
1  Per-store results are not in the briefing pack; closure costs for the six lapsing leases (staff, write-offs) are not given and would also count against the $25M limit

slides.title: Management's hours cut protects the covenant, but shrink and the wage rise would erase its saving by FY2028

paragraphs.text: 1 Diagnosis    2 Gross margin    3 Losses    4 Plan
Management's hours cut protects the covenant, but shrink and the wage rise would erase its saving by FY2028
Net operating-income effect of management's draft plan, $ millions a year, FY2028 run-rate
saving a year from 8% fewer scheduled store hours (management estimate)
gross profit lost if shrink rises 0.5 pp of sales, as it did when hours per sales dollar fell 6%
2027 minimum-wage rise of 4% on the remaining store labor
carrier's proposed 3% rise, with e-commerce frozen at today's size
net gain left by FY2028: effectively nothing
The cut is fast, which is why it appeals, but it leaves the real causes in place
▪	In FY2026 the plan would bring operating income to $22–29.5M, clear of the $20M covenant
▪	By FY2028 margin would sit at 1.0–1.5% of sales; the high end assumes shrink does not rise at all
▪	The freeze keeps the e-commerce loss of about $10.4M a year, and promotions and shrink are untouched
▪	A smaller cut of about 4% of hours, taken only from the most-staffed stores after shrink is fixed, is the better use of the idea
Keep a targeted hours cut as the lever that closes the gap to 3.0%, not as the plan's first move
1  Shrink risk uses the FY2023–25 pattern; the leanest quartile already runs 0.8 percentage points above the best-staffed
Sources: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); team analysis
